assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work gave trade policy a rigorous political-economy foundation. The protection-for-sale model, with the companion work on endogenous growth and trade, shaped both theory and empirical testing. It sits at the core of the field and has changed how economists understand tariff formation and lobbying.
assessment.attribution: The credit is concentrated in the Grossman-Helpman partnership, whose joint papers and book define the contribution. I would propose both, since adding anyone else would dilute a clean attribution. Helpman also appears in the firm-heterogeneity candidate, so I treat this ballot as the broader theoretical contribution.
assessment.maturity: The central results date from the 1990s and have had decades of empirical testing and extension. Trade has not been recognised since 2008. Timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions is mixed and depends on the setting.
The committee may prefer to reward trade through the firm-heterogeneity line instead.
My view of how the endogenous-growth work should be weighted is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The credit-cycles model shows how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It underpins much modern macro-finance and the policy discussion of financial amplification. The conceptual contribution is deep and widely used.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 Kiyotaki-Moore paper is the clear anchor, so two laureates are cleanly justified. Gertler and Gilchrist, with Bernanke, built the parallel financial-accelerator line. A third name would be defensible but weakens a tidy citation, and the 2022 prize already recognised Bernanke.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years of influence, plus renewed relevance after 2008. Very mature.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may reduce the committee's appetite for another financial-frictions award.
The boundary of credit to the financial-accelerator tradition is contestable.
The prize is based mainly on one landmark paper.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Demand estimation with random coefficients and dynamic industry models turned industrial organisation into a quantitative, policy-relevant discipline. It is used routinely in merger review, antitrust and regulation. The methodological reach into other fields is substantial.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand-system contribution is clearly Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes. Pakes also made independent dynamic contributions with Ericson and Benkard. Bresnahan's earlier new-empirical-IO work and Reiss's are foundational but sit in a different contribution. The 'three at most' limit forces a hard choice, so attribution is the main difficulty.
assessment.maturity: The core methods date from 1994-95 and have been used for three decades, with strong validation in practice.
uncertainties: Whether the citation should be the BLP triple or include Bresnahan.
Some of the identification assumptions are strong and debated.
It is unclear whether the committee views this as a methods or an applied-IO prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence changed the understanding of labour-market adjustment, wage inequality and the distributional costs of trade. The work has had unusually wide policy influence. It combines conceptual framing with credible local-labour-market designs.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock work is Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The earlier task-based framework is Autor with Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu and Restrepo have related contributions. The ballot omits some who shaped the task approach, so the attribution is cleaner for the trade-shock work than for technology.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock papers date from 2013 onward, and the task literature from the early 2000s. There have been many replications and critiques, and the shift-share identification debate is still being worked through.
uncertainties: Shift-share identification and the exposure designs have been questioned.
Task-model credit overlaps with Acemoglu's work, which the 2024 prize did not specifically cover.
Whether the long-run adjustment findings will hold up.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top incomes, built from tax records, opened up the study of inequality, and the research reshaped public debate and the research agenda. The data contribution is major. The theoretical and causal interpretation is more contested than the measurement.
assessment.attribution: Piketty-Saez is the core of the top-income-share work. Zucman's work on offshore wealth is newer and builds on the same methods. Saez also appears in the optimal-taxation candidate, so there is overlap across ballots. I would limit the citation to the original measurement partnership.
assessment.maturity: The top-income series date from the early 2000s, and the wealth-distribution extensions are more recent. The measurement is well established, but the interpretation of wealth-taxation and r>g claims is still contested.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the top-share and wealth estimates, including the treatment of tax avoidance and retained earnings.
Weight on the measurement contribution versus the theory.
Possible split of credit between this ballot and the optimal-taxation one.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with the Phillips curve, interest-rate rules and optimal monetary policy, is the workhorse of central-bank analysis. Its practical and academic reach is very large. The intellectual lineage is long and also includes contributions already recognised by earlier prizes.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main obstacle. At least eight names are listed, and the contributions are layered: Calvo pricing, Taylor rules, the DSGE estimation work of Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, Smets-Wouters, Gali-Gertler, and Woodford's synthesis. Three names will leave out important people. I pick Woodford, Gali and Taylor as the most representative of framework, estimation and policy rule.
assessment.maturity: The framework has been dominant for twenty-five years, though the post-2020 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique have tested it.
uncertainties: No tidy three-person attribution exists.
The Lucas, Sargent-Sims and Kydland-Prescott prizes already cover parts of the lineage.
Reassessment of the framework after the recent inflation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population administrative data have been used to measure intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and returns to policy at a scale and credibility that were not previously possible. The work has had a large influence on empirical practice and public policy. It builds on and extends the register-data tradition.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the dominant figure. Hendren and Friedman are central co-authors on different strands, and Katz is an earlier contributor on neighbourhood effects. Because Chetty overlaps with the optimal-taxation ballot, the credit is spread, and a three-name citation would be hard to defend cleanly.
assessment.maturity: Most of the work was published after 2014. Influence is already very high, but the long-run replication and policy evidence is still accumulating. Some causal neighbourhood claims are recent.
uncertainties: The work may be early relative to typical prize timing.
Attribution to a team-science enterprise and the division of credit among the co-authors.
Some mobility-measurement and neighbourhood-effect findings have been debated for sensitivity to method.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic factor models and diffusion-index forecasting gave macroeconomics practical tools to use large datasets, and the same authors contributed to the study of instability, structural VARs and identification. The methods are standard in central banks and in empirical macro. The conceptual novelty is real, but the work is more of a toolkit than a single discovery.
assessment.attribution: Stock and Watson are the clear centre of the diffusion-index and factor-forecasting work. Reichlin and co-authors developed the generalised dynamic factor approach in parallel, and Diebold, Mariano and West made contributions on forecast evaluation. A two-person citation would leave out legitimate parallel contributors.
assessment.maturity: The central papers date from 2002 and earlier, and use is well established. Recent machine-learning forecasting methods have somewhat reduced the uniqueness of the contribution.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees a prize-sized discovery rather than a set of methods.
The parallel European factor-model work complicates attribution.
Stock also appears in the weak-instruments candidate, which splits credit.
